g.text: One immutable 50 KB object, and one mutable 500-byte row per recipient
Store them together and you pay 4x on storage AND rewrite 50 KB every time somebody marks an email read.

THE CENTRAL TABLE one row per (recipient, message) - small and mutable
the key: partition, then time-sortable clustering

~1,640 PB / YEAR saved, from one modelling decision.
Why message_uuid is a TIMEUUID - one property doing three jobs
CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_uuid DESC) means the
newest messages are physically first in the partition,
so 'most recent 50' is a range scan that stops
immediately. No sort, no separate index.
any web server or processing worker generates one
locally - no counter, no allocator, no round trip.
pagination is a cursor, not an offset
'give me 50 more, older than this uuid' is simply a
Compare the URL shortener, which explicitly REJECTS
time-based IDs because it needs short codes. Here there
is no length constraint, so the trade flips entirely -
same technique, opposite verdict, from one differing
Why the partition key is (user_id, folder_id) and not just user_id
ORDER BY message_uuid DESC LIMIT 50; -- ONE partition, ONE range scan
With user_id alone, all of one user's mail is ONE partition. For a mailbox with
two million messages that partition is enormous - and in a wide-column store the
partition is the unit of storage AND of repair, so unbounded growth is an
operational problem before it is a storage one. Adding folder_id bounds it and,
more importantly, matches the dominant query exactly.
the cost: moving a message between folders is a DELETE plus an INSERT
Because the folder is part of the partition key, a different folder is a different partition. A genuine cost, and acceptable
for two reasons: listing a folder is vastly more frequent than moving a message, and the row being moved is ~500 bytes rather
than 50 KB - THE BODY DOES NOT MOVE, ONLY THE POINTER DOES. Which is where separating content from state pays off a second
Why read/unread needs a whole second table
mail arrives -> INSERT into messages_by_folder AND unread_by_folder
user marks read -> UPDATE is_read in messages_by_folder
DELETE from unread_by_folder <- the row simply leaves
user marks unread -> re-INSERT into unread_by_folder
Cassandra-family stores cannot efficiently filter on a non-key column, so
WHERE is_read = false would mean fetching the whole folder and filtering in
memory. Fine for 50 messages, unusable for a mailbox with a million. So the
trade is explicit: DUPLICATED STORAGE AND A WRITE-TIME CONSISTENCY OBLIGATION,
in exchange for a query that would otherwise be impossible.
The honest risk is drift: a partial failure leaves a row in unread_by_folder
that messages_by_folder says is read. That presents as a WRONG UNREAD BADGE -
confusing rather than harmful - and it is why the unread count is periodically
recomputed rather than trusted indefinitely. Naming it as a known drift with a
known repair beats pretending the denormalization is free.
body_hash = sha256(canonicalized body) - three payoffs from one indirection
the same corporate slide deck forwarded around a
company is stored once regardless of how many
distinct emails carry it - so the saving is larger
marking read touches ~500 bytes, not 50 KB
because the mutable row and the immutable content
The cost is REFERENCE COUNTING, and it is the part that needs care. Content can only be reclaimed when the last recipient
deletes their copy, so either maintain a refcount (correct, and a hot contended row for a widely-forwarded attachment) or run
a periodic mark-and-sweep collector (cheaper, and reclaims late). The GC approach is the right default here for the same
reason the object-storage case study takes it: ORPHANED BYTES ARE CHEAP, AND A DANGLING POINTER IS DATA LOSS. Delete the
metadata row immediately; reclaim the content later.
Threading is best-effort, and always will be
References carries the whole ancestry, so a thread_id can be assigned by looking
up whether any referenced Message-Id already belongs to a thread - and if so,
But some clients omit References, some mangle it, and mailing lists rewrite
headers - so providers fall back on heuristics: normalized subject matching
(stripping Re:/Fwd:), participant overlap, time proximity. Which means threading
occasionally merges unrelated conversations or splits one. Inherent to a
federated protocol where you do not control the sender, and the reason threading
is a BONUS requirement rather than a guarantee.
Consistency chosen over availability - affordable only because of a protocol from 1982
message content IMMUTABLE once written content-addressed, so the hash IS the identity: no consistency
question can arise, because a hash always maps to the same bytes
per-recipient metadata row STRONG within its partition a message acknowledged with 250 OK must be durably present.
is_read / is_starred / labels EVENTUAL, last-write-wins two devices setting the same boolean write the same value, so LWW
is CORRECT rather than a compromise - no coordination needed
folder_id (a move) EVENTUAL, last-write-wins two devices moving one message resolve to one winner, pushed to
both over WebSocket. A conflict-resolution UI would be worse.
unread_by_folder EVENTUAL w.r.t. the main table denormalized; drifts on partial failure, repaired by recompute
unread_count EVENTUAL, drifts incrementally maintained, periodically recomputed
search index EVENTUAL, seconds behind async, with a hybrid recent-message scan to cover the gap
Because 'data loss is unacceptable' outranks availability, a metadata partition that loses quorum STOPS SERVING rather than
accepting writes it might lose. So during a failover, affected users briefly cannot read or receive mail - and that is the
correct trade, because SMTP senders will retry for days. THE PROTOCOL'S OWN RETRY BEHAVIOUR IS WHAT MAKES CHOOSING
CONSISTENCY AFFORDABLE, which is a nice example of a constraint from 1982 buying you something.
Partition by user_id everywhere - and why each alternative fails
one user's mail scatters across every node, so a folder listing becomes a full-cluster
scatter-gather. Fatal for the dominant query.
threads span users - that is what makes them conversations - so this reintroduces
cross-user partitions and does not bound partition size either.
all inbound mail hits the newest partition. The classic write hotspot.
Two structural gaps worth naming as gaps rather than as backlog. A GENUINELY SHARED MAILBOX DOES NOT FIT: support@company.com
read by twelve people is one mailbox with twelve readers, and user_id partitioning assumes an email belongs to one user. The
pseudo-user workaround breaks per-user read state, which is exactly what a shared inbox needs most. And END-TO-END ENCRYPTION
IS STRUCTURALLY INCOMPATIBLE WITH THIS SCHEMA, not merely unbuilt: content-addressed dedup requires the server to see
identical plaintext to compute identical hashes, search indexing requires reading bodies, threading requires reading headers,
and spam filtering requires reading everything. E2EE would forfeit the 1,640 PB/year saving, server-side search and spam
filtering simultaneously. Alongside them: content reference counting is unresolved (no sweep interval, and no answer for an
attachment whose reference set spans millions of users' partitions), and unread drift has a repair but no DETECTION - a
systematic bug in the dual write would be invisible until users complained about badges.
